title: Even after death (2:11)
hook: if the one you wronged has died, go to the grave with ten people and confess
tomorrow: can one small deed really tip the whole world?

segments.voice: Last time: forgive readily, the job of the one who's asked. Ask, and be easy to win over. But that whole road assumes both people are still here to walk it.

The contact is still in the phone. The thread ends where it ended, on something sharp, and the reply that was supposed to come later never came, because later ran out. A funeral, a casserole, a lot of people saying kind things. And underneath, a sentence nobody can deliver now. A gentle note before we go on: today is about someone who has died, so take it at your own pace. What if the person you hurt is gone? Maimonides doesn't shrug. He gives directions.
screen: `THE THREAD ENDS ON SOMETHING SHARP.` → `LATER RAN OUT.` → `HE GIVES DIRECTIONS.`

segments.voice: If someone wronged a person who died before they could ask forgiveness, he writes, they bring ten people and stand them at the grave. And there they say: I sinned against the Lord, God of Israel, and against this person, and this is what I did to them. Three details are worth slowing down for. First, the ten. That's the same number as a minyan, the gathering needed for communal prayer. The apology that couldn't be private now becomes public, with witnesses standing in the cold. Second, the words have two addresses: God, and the person. A wrong against someone is also a wrong against the One who made them, and the confession names both. Third, the practical part. If money was owed, it goes to the heirs. If there are no heirs anyone knows of, it's left with the beit din, the court, and the confession is made. Maimonides doesn't say what the one who died hears. He says what the living one does. And the shape of it is clear: death closes a conversation, but it doesn't close the door of return. The apology can still be made, the debt can still be paid, and the wrong can still be named out loud, even after death.
screen: `TEN PEOPLE AT THE GRAVE.` · `AGAINST GOD AND AGAINST THEM.` · `WHAT WAS OWED GOES TO THE HEIRS.` · `THE DOOR DOESN'T CLOSE.` · then, large: `EVEN AFTER DEATH.`

segments.voice: Look at one thing that belonged to, or reminds you of, someone who's gone: a photo, a name in your phone, an object on a shelf. If no one comes to mind, choose someone you've simply lost touch with. In your heart, say the sentence you never got to say, and stay with it as long as feels right.
screen: `ONE PHOTO, ONE NAME.` · `THE SENTENCE YOU NEVER SAID.`

segments.voice: Even after death: Maimonides' path when the one you wronged has died. Ten people at the grave, both wrongs named, and any debt paid to the heirs.
Your line: even after death. The conversation ends; the return doesn't have to. Go gently today.

howItsDone: Following Maimonides, someone who wronged a person who has died may gather a minyan at the grave to ask forgiveness; some also visit graves before the High Holy Days.
